blocks.p: Dear Stephen, there were eleven of us in Tobin’s bunkroom tonight. Two fell asleep and one of them snored. Nobody had a robe, nobody knew the words, and the tea was terrible. It was the finest service I have ever attended, and I have attended thousands.
Galatia received him as if he were an angel, which was the more remarkable because he arrived on a stretcher.

He seized coming out of stasis in the arrival hold at Highfold, before the frost was off the lid of his pod, in front of thirty strangers. Lucan had warned him it might happen. He woke two days later in a stone house half sunk into the ground, with the wind going over the roof like surf, and the first face he saw was Teo Thorne’s. Teo had flown second seat on the run, on Hollis’s say-so and not Lucan’s: a master could carry a trainee as ballast crew on a short run without any clearance at all, and Lyda, who had stalled his clearance for a year, had found that she could not stall Hollis. He was meant to go straight back with the ship. He had carried Sol off it instead and stayed. Lyda, Tobin said, would have something to say about that.

Galatia was not one place but a scatter of them, a dozen settlements across a high plateau so wide that the crawlers took a day to run between any two. There was nothing on it but wind and tussock grass the color of a lion’s back, every blade bent the same way, and herds of shaggy, patient beasts that the Galatians sheared and milked and talked to. The people were broad and red-faced and loud, and they did everything with their whole bodies. The renewal clinic came round once a year by crawler, when the passes were open, and half of them had never troubled to meet it.

They knew what a fit was. Their grandmothers had called it the falling sickness, and no one in Highfold had ever thought to report it to anyone. Nan Corrie, the herd-mistress who had taken him in, told him so on the third day, sitting on the end of his bed with a bowl of something hot and sour.

“Saw you go down,” she said. “Saw what they did, them on the ship, backing off. We don’t do that here.” She pushed the bowl at him. “If you’d needed my eyes, Bishop, I’d have had them out for you. Eat.”

He preached to them first from that bed, because he could not yet stand, to as many as could crowd into the room, and they listened as no cathedral had ever listened to him: with their elbows on their knees, arguing, laughing, sometimes weeping, which they did as loudly as everything else. By the end of the sixth week there were churches in four settlements, Highfold and Tarn and Cold Ash and Stannery, and Sol had stood waist deep in a dozen freezing stock ponds and brought up sixty people dark. They were the first churches that were his. They sent him on with everything they had: cheese, wool, a coat so heavy he could barely lift his arms in it, and Nan Corrie on the crawler step howling like a child, without the least embarrassment, until the wind took the sound away.
The noise found them before he left.

It came first to a herder named Cai, nineteen, whose small sister had died in the winter and come back Not received. A week after his baptism, he came to Sol’s door at midnight, grey-faced. It had been talking to him in his own voice, he said, over and over, with a crackle under it. She’s in the holding light. She’s waiting. Go back and they’ll let her through. Go back. Go back.
“Say the name,” Sol told him, as Tobin had told him. “Say it till it breaks.”

Cai said it, and it broke. By the time Sol left, every house in Highfold knew what to say in the dark. The children knew it best. They had never seen an old man except in pictures, and they called Sol Granda, and he let them.

Before they left Highfold, Teo asked to be washed. He had flown second seat on the Galatia run and stayed to carry Sol when Sol could not carry himself, and he had sat at the back of every crowded room with his chin on his knees, saying nothing. He asked on the last evening, in the stock pond below Nan Corrie’s house, with the wind flattening the grass all the way to the edge of the sky. Sol stood in the cold brown water to his waist and poured it over the boy three times, in the words Tobin had taught him, and Teo came up gasping and laughing and put both hands to his temple, and said, “It’s gone quiet,” in the voice of someone who has just set down a load he did not know he was carrying. He made Sol promise not to tell his sister. Sol promised, and did not like it.
Dr. Lucan met them at Berea, and stayed.

Berea’s sun never rose or set. The world kept one face to it, and the settlement lay in a band of perpetual evening on the edge between the burnt side and the frozen one, under a red sun that sat forever on the rim of the hills. The colonists were descended from a survey corps that had come to map the system and never left. Their houses were full of instruments. They kept ledgers of rainfall and births and the depth of the frost, and they were not impressed by anything.

“You’ll forgive us,” said Ione Vey, the station archivist, a narrow grey-eyed woman with ink on her fingers. “We’ve had a great many people come through here to tell us things. We’d like to read it ourselves.”

So they read it. Every evening, which on Berea was the only time there was, they gathered at the long tables in the archive with the lamps lit and Stephen’s copy open in the middle, and they checked everything Sol said against it. When he paraphrased, they corrected him. When he said he said, someone found the page or wrote down that they could not. They laid the Book of Life beside it, line by line, and made a ledger of the places where one said a thing and the other was silent, and the ledger grew to forty pages, and then to a hundred. In the beginning was Life, on one side. In the beginning was the Word, on the other. Ione Vey ran her inked finger from one to the other and said nothing at all for some time.
Lucan sat with them every night until the lamps were trimmed. “These are my people,” he said once, to no one in particular, writing.
They found Stephen’s blanks, the places where the old pages had been unreadable and no seizure had given him the words, and asked Sol what was missing. He said he did not know.
“Good,” Ione Vey said. “If you’d said you knew, I’d have stopped listening.”

In the fifth week they began to copy it. Six of them sat at the long table with paper the archive had been hoarding for a century and wrote it out by hand, slowly, checking every line against every other, so that each copy could be carried to a world Sol would never reach.

The noise came to Berea, as it came everywhere, but it found the Bereans hard going. A surveyor named Wyn Aske woke one evening certain he remembered a passage, clearly, word for word, in which the man in the book had said that the ascended were kept safe in the light and no one need ever go into the dark. It was so clear that he wept with relief. Then he got up and went to the archive and opened the copy and looked for it, and it was not there. He looked for two hours. Then he wrote down in the ledger, in his small surveyor’s hand, False memory. Not in the text, and went back to bed.
That was how Berea fought it. They checked.

Once, near the end, he read them a passage from the prophets only because it came next. It was one of the places where Stephen’s pen had pressed so hard that the letters stood up from the paper under Sol’s thumb. How you have fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of the dawn. How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low. You said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven. Above the stars of God I will set my throne on high. I will make myself like the Most High.
No one corrected him. Outside the long windows the red sun sat on the rim of the hills, where it always sat.
“Whom is it about?” Ione Vey said.
Sol looked at the page. Something had wanted a throne above the stars and been thrown down for it, and Stephen had copied every word of it as though it might get away from him. Sol did not know why.
“I don’t know,” he said.
Ione Vey wrote it in the ledger, in her small inked hand, as she wrote everything down: Asked whom. Not known. Then she turned the page.

“Forty-six,” Lucan said, on their last evening there. He had a set of calipers and a lamp and a table of figures he had drawn up himself, and he measured Sol at every port: the skin at the back of the hand, the eyes, the grey. He wrote it down. Sol’s knees had begun to hurt on stairs, and on Berea there were a great many stairs.
Korinna was appetite.

The port sat on a neck of land between two seas, and ships too big to go round were hauled across it on the Drag, a slipway of greased rails a dozen kilometers long, day and night, to the shriek of winches and the shouting of the haulers. The town lived on the traffic. It was built of gaming halls and eating houses and arcades that never closed, and in its back alleys were renewal shops that would renew anyone who could pay, cheaply and badly, so that people on Korinna died of cheap renewals as well as of drink and knives, and no one minded much. It was hot. Everything smelled of grease and frying and the sea.

The church there grew faster than anywhere, and harder. Within a month there were a hundred, and factions. Some said they belonged to Tobin, because Tobin had baptized them. Some said they belonged to the bishop. A hauler named Ruel had begun having fits at meetings, loud and theatrical ones that Lucan watched with his mouth tight and later called, in the record, not epilepsy, and after each one Ruel had new words that were not in any book, and a following of his own. At the shared meal the warehouse owners came early and ate, and the haulers came off shift late to empty pots.

Sol lost his temper. He could not remember ever having done it, and it astonished him. He stood up in the long room above the chandler’s shop where they met, with the din of the Drag coming through the shutters, and heard his own voice go up like a bell, and could not stop it. Then he stopped. He opened Stephen’s copy and read them, in a voice that shook, the passage he had marked on the crossing: Love is patient and kind. Love does not envy or boast. It is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way. He read it to the end. The room was very quiet. A warehouse owner named Benedek got up and took his plate and went and sat on the floor among the haulers, and after a while two or three others did.

It was not enough. He knew it was not. He stayed on Korinna nine weeks, longer than anywhere, and left it a church still full of quarrels, and loved it more than any of the others, and could not have said why.
He lost Dace Morrow there.

Dace was a dice-runner from the arcades, quick and funny and frightened of everything, and Sol had baptized him in the harbor among the hulls. Three weeks after, the noise came for him and did not let go. Sol did not know that until Dace came to the meeting one night smiling, with his color back and his hands steady, and told them all cheerfully that it had been a fever.
“Went to a shop on the Drag,” he said. “Back room. Twenty minutes. It came back on.” He touched his temple. “The hum. You forget how nice it is. It was like being let in out of the cold.”

Sol looked at him and saw the Bounty Market looking back: the bright, untroubled face of a man who had not lost anything because he could no longer feel it go. Dace shook his hand warmly on the way out and wished him well.

Sol went down to the harbor afterward and sat on a bollard among the hulls, where he had stood in the water with Dace’s head in his hands, and found that it was possible to grieve for someone who was still alive.
Ephes was gold.

Its city climbed in white terraces from a warm green sea to the Cathedral of the Window at its crown, and the cathedral’s Window was the largest outside Sion, so bright that ships came in by it at night. Pilgrims came from twenty worlds to see their ascended in it. The whole city lived on them. Every stair was lined with stalls selling household Windows and their gilded frames and little gold ascension tokens stamped with the great Window’s shape, and every third family in Ephes belonged to the guild of Windowsmiths. On those stairs pilgrims looked at Sol’s grey head and drew their children aside, and he heard the word go up the steps ahead of him: denied. Lucan’s calipers said forty-eight.

The faith came to Ephes through the pilgrims who had climbed all those stairs to see their dead and seen only holding light. It spread among them, and then into the city, and then into the guild, and in the eighth month after Concord a Windowsmith named Niko Brandt and forty others carried their household Windows down to the square below the cathedral. They had pried them out of their alcoves. They switched them off and laid them face down on the white stones in rows. A guild clerk walked along the rows with a tablet and reckoned their worth aloud, and it came to more than a smith earned in ten years.

Two days later the guildmaster, Harl Dorrance, called the smiths together in the old amphitheater by the harbor. Sol heard afterward what he said. Not only their trade, but the Window itself, the great Window of Ephes that all the Diaspora came to see, was being despised, and by a heretic who had been a bishop. The crowd took up the response from the ascension rite and would not let it go. Life without end. Life without end. They chanted it for two hours. Most of them, Lucan said later, did not know why they had come.

Someone found Niko Brandt in the street, and Tobin with him, and they were dragged into the amphitheater. Sol tried to go in after them. Six of the believers held him by the arms and the back of his coat on the steps outside, and the Berean copy Ione Vey had pressed on him fell into the dust between his feet.
“They’ll tear you apart,” one of them said into his ear, “and then they’ll know they can.”

Tobin came out on his own, bloody and slow, because he was too big to hold. Niko Brandt was carried out an hour later, after the colony’s provost had stood on the amphitheater wall and told the crowd, in a dry, carrying voice, that the men they had dragged in had robbed no one, that the courts sat on the fourth day if the guild had a grievance, and that she would be asked to account for this afternoon to people who were not as patient as she was. The crowd went home. Niko had been kicked in the head.

He was dark. The cathedral could not renew him and would not have tried. Lucan did what could be done without a surgeon’s theater, which was nothing, and said so. Niko lay three days in a back room above his own shuttered shop, sometimes knowing them and sometimes not. On the third night he asked Sol to tell him again about the garden, and Sol told him: the woman weeping, the man she took for the gardener, her name. Niko smiled at that. He died before morning, with his wife Hedda holding one hand and Sol the other.

On Ephes every body went down to reclamation beneath the cathedral. The believers would not let him go there. They wrapped him in a sheet and carried him on a door out of the city and up the bare hill above the sea, where nothing had ever been buried, and dug a grave with borrowed tools. None of them had ever dug one. It took most of the afternoon.

People followed them up from the city to watch, as if to something obscene. By the time the hole was deep enough there were hundreds on the slope, and wardens in white at the edge of them, standing very still.

Sol stood at the head of the grave with Stephen’s copy in his hands. He read what Stephen had said to him in the white cell, in its place now, where it belonged. I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live. Then he tried to say something of his own and could not. He told them instead about the shortest sentence in the book. A man stood at his friend’s grave, knowing he was about to raise him. And Jesus wept.
Then Sol wept, a bishop of Life, in the open, on a hill above Ephes, in front of a crowd and the wardens of the church.

They all did. Hedda Brandt sank down by the grave and keened, a high raw sound no one on that hill had ever heard. Tobin wept the way he always did, without shame, like rain. Benedek, who had followed them from Korinna, wept with his big hands hanging at his sides, and Lucan stood with his record book closed against his chest and his face wet and did not seem to know it. They said the shepherd’s psalm together, badly, out of time, as the old ones must have said it. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Then they let Niko down on ropes and filled the grave in.

The wardens did not move. The provost had reminded them that morning, Sol learned afterward, that a relay notice was not a warrant, and that no warrant of the Office ran this far out; there was nothing they could lawfully do but watch. And no one had ever taught them what to do about tears.

Someone on the slope began to jeer and stopped. Then, near the front of the crowd, a woman in a pilgrim’s pale coat put her hands over her face. Her son, Sol learned later, had been in the holding light for two years. She stood there among the watchers and wept, and after a while she came down the hill, stumbling a little on the stones, and stood with them at the grave.
It was the first funeral on Ephes in four hundred years. It was, Sol thought afterward, the first time in all those years that he had truly worshiped.

Below them the city was going gold in the evening, and the great Window was lit for the pilgrims. Up on the hill, in the open, among the dark Halos and the turned earth, a woman wept for her son, and no one asked her to stop.
